purpose: Prevents unauthorized reading or modification of specific properties within an object, even when overall object-level authorization is correctly enforced.
summary: Broken Object Property Level Authorization combines two related issues: excessive data exposure, where the API returns more object properties than the client should see, and mass assignment, where the API blindly accepts client-supplied fields and updates properties the user should not be able to change.
expectedStatementElements: How API responses are filtered to return only the properties the requesting user is authorized to see, rather than the full object
How the API validates which fields a client is allowed to set or update, rather than blindly binding all submitted fields
Whether sensitive or privileged properties (e.g., role, isAdmin, balance) are protected from client-side modification
How the API is tested for excessive data exposure and mass assignment specifically
evidenceExamples: API response schema showing explicit allow-listed properties per endpoint/role
Input validation or DTO (data transfer object) code showing which fields can be set on update
Test results attempting to modify a privileged field (like role or admin flag) via a standard update request
Documentation of sensitive properties and which roles can read or write them
commonGaps: API responses return entire internal objects, including fields the client shouldn't see
Update endpoints blindly bind all submitted JSON fields to the object, including ones users shouldn't be able to set
Sensitive fields like role or account balance can be modified through a generic update endpoint
No testing has attempted to submit unexpected fields to see if they get applied
interviewQuestions: Does this endpoint's response include any fields the requesting user shouldn't be able to see?
If I added an extra field like 'role': 'admin' to my update request, would it get applied?
Which fields are explicitly allow-listed for client updates, versus everything just being accepted?
Has anyone tried submitting unexpected fields to see what the API actually does with them?
